script.title: Why Japan Called Them the Black Ships

lines: An American commodore sailed four smoking warships into Edo Bay.
Their black smoke deeply frightened the Japanese.
This was Matthew Perry, in 1853.
Japan called his fleet the Black Ships.
But the name was older.
In 1543, Portuguese traders reached Japan.
Their giant carracks weighed 1200 to 1600 tons.
Each hull was painted black with pitch.
Black Ships meant every Western ship.
But why paint a hull black?
Weeds and barnacles grow on ship hulls.
Plutarch wrote that weeds and filth made a ship weak.
Fouling can raise drag by up to 60 percent.
You see, it's like running in a soaking wet coat.
So sailors coated hulls in Black stuff, a mix of tar and pitch.
But did it stop weeds?
It may only have fought shipworms that bore into wood.
In 1761, HMS Alarm was covered in copper.
Copper made a poisonous film that kept weed away.
From about 1770, the Royal Navy coppered its whole fleet.
And Perry's Black Ships?
Their hulls were not even black.
Their coal-fired engines belched black smoke.
Yet their arrival reopened Japan after more than 200 years of isolation.

claims.claim: The sight of the four ships entering Edo Bay, belching black smoke, deeply frightened the Japanese; the expedition was under the command of Commodore Matthew C. Perry in 1853.
In 1543 Portuguese traders arrived in Japan; carracks of 1200 to 1600 tons engaged in this trade had the hull painted black with pitch, and the term came to apply for all western vessels.
Plutarch explained that when weeds, ooze and filth stick upon a ship's sides, the stroke of the ship is more obtuse and weak; biofouling can increase drag by up to 60%.

Before the 18th century, Black stuff, a mixture of tar and pitch, was used; there is dispute whether such treatments were actual anti-fouling techniques or were intended to combat wood-boring shipworms.

The first copper sheathing experiments were made in 1761 on HMS Alarm; the copper produced a poisonous film that deterred marine creatures, and from about 1770 the Royal Navy coppered the bottoms of the entire fleet.
Though the hulls of Perry's ships were not black, their coal-fired steam engines belched black smoke; the kurofune became a symbol of the end of isolation after more than two hundred years.

cast.perry: a 59 year old American naval commodore, heavy build, a broad fleshy clean shaven face, thick dark brown hair swept forward, a stern frown, a dark navy blue frock coat with gold epaulettes and brass buttons, 1850s
cast.samurai: a 35 year old Japanese samurai official, slim build, a shaved crown with a black oiled topknot, a narrow clean shaven face, a dark indigo kimono, grey striped hakama trousers and two swords at the waist, 1850s
cast.captain: a 40 year old Portuguese sea captain, tall, olive skin, a long forked black beard, a black velvet cap, a deep crimson doublet with puffed sleeves and a white ruffled shirt, 1540s
cast.sailor: a 25 year old Portuguese sailor, wiry build, a shaved bald head, a thin black moustache, a loose cream canvas shirt with torn sleeves and brown baggy knee breeches, barefoot, 1540s
cast.plutarch: a 60 year old Greek writer, slender, curly white hair, a full curly white beard, a calm lined face, a pale sky blue tunic under a cream wool cloak, 1st century AD
cast.shipwright: a 50 year old English shipwright, stout, a ruddy round face, a grey tied-back wig, a brown wool coat with sleeves rolled up and a black leather apron, 1760s
